OwnBridge is an open-source tool for deploying a private VPN. All you need is a VPS with a public IPv4 address. With just a few simple setup steps, you can deploy a private VPN network that you fully control and that supports multiple protocols.

The core components used by OwnBridge are based on mature open-source projects from the Internet. It currently supports common protocols such as Shadowsocks (SS), VLESS, and Hysteria 2 (HY2). These protocols have mature client ecosystems and are widely used in private network connectivity scenarios.

The OwnBridge app code and server deployment scripts are publicly available for anyone to inspect. Developers can review them and suggest improvements. Download the app from the official OwnBridge GitHub Releases page and verify the source before installing it. Every deployment step is visible, so you can use it with greater confidence.
OwnBridge can generate connection profiles for Clash / Mihomo and v2rayN / v2rayNG. You can continue using these clients while connecting directly to your own private VPN nodes.

Compared with shared proxy or VPN services, private deployment offers greater autonomy and control. Your server, nodes, accounts, and configurations remain under your own management. You can reinstall, migrate, change the IP address, or destroy the server whenever needed. Because your node is not shared with large numbers of unknown users, private deployment also reduces your exposure to third-party proxy providers that may record, analyze, or retain connection information. As a result, resource availability, operating conditions, bandwidth performance, and privacy controls are generally more predictable.

Private deployment, however, does not mean absolute security or absolute anonymity. Your VPS provider, network operator, and the websites or services you access may still record certain connection information at their respective layers of the network. The primary value of a private VPN is greater control and reduced dependence on third-party proxy services—not the promise of an untraceable or completely anonymous network.

OwnBridge is a deployment tool. It does not operate VPN servers, sell network access, or provide shared proxy nodes. You purchase and manage your own VPS and are responsible for ensuring that your deployment and use comply with applicable laws and regulations, your VPS provider’s terms, and the policies of the networks you use.

When purchasing a VPS, make sure it includes a usable public IPv4 address. If your provider also offers IPv6 addresses, it is generally worth keeping them. When both your local network and client device support IPv6 connectivity, IPv6 can serve as an additional connection path and, in some situations, as a fallback when IPv4 connectivity is unavailable.

Before deployment, make sure your server runs an Ubuntu version supported by this app; the plan page will check the exact version. For a private VPN used by a small number of personal devices, 1 vCPU and 512 MB of RAM are typically sufficient for basic use. If you plan to run multiple protocols, a management panel, or additional services on the same server, 1 GB of RAM or more is recommended.

To minimize conflicts with existing software, ports, or system configurations, we recommend deploying OwnBridge on a fresh VPS. After deployment, change the server\'s root password promptly and store your login credentials securely. Where possible, we also recommend configuring SSH key authentication and disabling unnecessary remote login methods.
If you have not purchased a VPS yet, visit our Server Recommendations page for suggested server specifications and providers suitable for OwnBridge deployments.

IPv4 works on most home and mobile networks, making it a practical first choice. Public IPv4 addresses are scarce, though, and a VPS may have only one. If that route is congested or the address becomes unreachable, you will need another way in. IPv4 alone does not promise low latency.

IPv6 has a much larger address space, and a server may have several IPv6 addresses to use as additional entry points. It may take a different route on IPv6-capable networks. The device and network you connect from must also support IPv6; having IPv6 on the server is not enough. IPv6 is not inherently faster or immune to blocking.

VLESS is highly flexible. It can pair with security options such as REALITY or TLS and different transport setups, balancing stability, compatibility, and room to grow. The downside is the number of settings: a simple task can turn into an engineering project. It is a good fit for a long-term primary node.

Shadowsocks has a simple design and low resource use. It is easy to deploy and maintain: a practical option that just gets running. Its built-in extension and traffic-disguise options are limited, so it fits lightweight personal use or a backup node.

Hysteria 2 runs on QUIC/UDP and suits high-latency routes, mild packet loss, and unstable cross-border links. With the right route, it can move large amounts of traffic quickly. A standard setup depends heavily on UDP; if the network restricts UDP, even a speedboat has to stay docked.

Here you choose a connection client, not a provider that supplies servers or routes. OwnBridge deploys nodes on your VPS; the client imports the generated configuration so your phone or computer can connect to them.\n\nThese open-source clients have established user communities and continue to be maintained. Their code and release history are public, so you can get the software from official release pages and choose or change your client. Together with a server you control, this makes the connection process more transparent and gives you more control.

A good fit if you want one configuration for multiple nodes and routing rules. Mihomo-based clients are available for Android and desktop. The downside is that “Clash” refers to many versions; older cores may not support every protocol or setting. Check the exact client before importing.

v2rayN is mainly for desktop, while v2rayNG is for Android. Node links and subscriptions offer a straightforward way to get started. They are separate apps, however, and support for protocols and transport options can vary by version and core. Each needs its own compatibility check.
